Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Game Overview 2 Goal of the Game 3 Gameplay 3.1 Preparation 3.2 A Turn 3.3 Consolidation 4 Key Elements 5 Game End & Scoring Game Overview During the Meiji era, Japan transforms into a modern industrial power, and you lead one of the great Zaibatsu conglomerates. Thematically, you guide the destiny of your corporation by building factories, developing new technologies, and dominating the domestic and export markets. Mechanically, you utilize an innovative worker-retrieval system where you take workers from action spaces to run your factories, with the color of the workers determining your efficiency during consolidation. Goal of the Game The goal is to accumulate the most victory points through industrial expansion and regional influence in Japan. The game ends when the influence tiles run out or the shipping track reaches its end. Gameplay Preparation Each player receives an individual board and starting capital in Yen. Factory blueprints and goods tiles are placed on the main board. Workers (meeples) are randomly distributed across the action spaces on the main board. A Turn On your turn, you must take exactly 1 worker from any action space and place it on your player board. Then, perform one of the actions associated with that space: Invest: Build a new factory or upgrade an existing one. Technology: Increase your technology level to produce more advanced goods. Production: Manufacture goods in up to 3 of your factories (costs coal). Market: Deliver goods to Japanese regions to place influence tiles. Export & Shipping: Sell goods overseas for bonuses or improve your shipping track. Consolidation Instead of taking a worker, you may choose to consolidate: Lose all unspent money and coal. Receive income (money and coal) based on your progress. Pay your workers. The more different colors you have collected, the higher the cost. Apply a multiplier to your end-game scoring conditions on your board. Key Elements Element Function Worker Color Determines costs during consolidation; sets of the same color are cheaper to maintain. Influence Calculated based on the value of the delivered goods and your shipping level. Good Tiers There are 3 levels (e.g., Silk and Paper up to Lightbulbs and Watches). Knowledge Grants access to blueprints and more efficient production methods. Game End & Scoring At the end of the game, majorities in the 4 regions of Japan are scored. Chosen multipliers on your player board determine how many points you receive for milestones (money, factories, exports). The player with the highest total score after this final tally wins. [Rating: 1/10] What's Your Game? are scammers, don't buy anything from them! (look up Madeira Kickstarter for evidence)

[Rating: 2/10] Definitely a gamer's game, which are generally too complex for my taste. This is one of the most complex I've ever played. From now on, I'll call such games "Kitchen Sink" games-- those which have everything but the kitchen sink thrown into them. Nippon is ultimately an area-control game, but to get there you have to deal with worker placement; coal, money and knowledge generation; building factories; producing goods; and various bonuses and enhancements. Way too many steps -- I'll take El Grande any day of the week.

[Rating: 2/10] Good player interaction, though there might be a runaway leader problem, and there is a strategy that appears to be immensely stronger and better than others. I'm too much of a novice to make determinations like that, however; my time with this was well spent, I'd like to learn the edges a bit more, but the gravitational pull isn't terribly strong.

[Rating: 3/10] Action selection and overall flow was actually neat, but the area majority on the main map totally wrecks it for me personally.

[Rating: 3/10] Nippon has some fantastic mechanics, namely the achievement-based bonus scoring structure and the way players attempt to minimize monetary penalties when retrieving workers during action selection. Mechanics like these are wrapped into some solid engine-building gameplay. Unfortunately, all this wonderful design is wasted in simplistic, completely uninspiring area control mechanics where the majority of the game's points are scored and entire engines can be crushed based on the whims of players. This makes Nippon one of the most disappointing games I've played.

[Rating: 3/10] Very tight,  frustrating, only 1 path to victory: other paths are tempting, but not strong enough

[Rating: 3/10] :star::star::nostar::nostar::nostar:  Very strategic Euro with area majority contests mixed in. The worker placement (or rather, worker removal) has a very interesting twist.  Great game, but not enough player interaction for my taste. And the late game can be restricting as you have establish your strategy at early and mid game.

[Rating: 3/10] This game is a complete and utter mess that needs consolidation. Don't make your friends suffer through it. It's using multiple layers of needless complexity to attempt to fix and correct it's poor design. It's a boardgame without language or action spaces that correspond with the flow of play. It's filled with symbology for resources that hold little communicative information. Seriously, find and play any other 18xx, economic sim, euro game etc. this one was the worst. Save yourself of 4 hours of doing homework reading a rulebook mid game.
